title: Design a Ride-Sharing Backend
subtitle: Combine location indexing, atomic matching, live updates, trip history, and payments
objectives: Handle a firehose of location updates without writing every one to a database
Search 'drivers near me' efficiently, and explain why a normal index can't do it
Design matching so one driver is never assigned to two riders
Reason about the whole trip lifecycle, and which parts tolerate being wrong

exercises.title: A location stream averages U/T updates per second
exercises.body: With U online drivers reporting every T seconds, average ingestion is U/T. Capacity must also cover bursts from synchronized timers, reconnects, and retries. Each accepted update replaces the driver's current coordinate while prior samples follow a separate archival path.
exercises.note: Durable trip history has a different access pattern; copy location events to an asynchronous stream so archival writes do not delay live updates.

exercises.prompt: A nearby-driver query scans 1,000,000 active drivers. Partition the map into cells and inspect only the rider's cell and its neighbors.
exercises.beforeStatus: DRIVERS EXAMINED · 1,000,000 for one nearby search
exercises.result: The search stopped scanning the whole city
exercises.why: A geospatial index maps locations into cells, limiting exact distance checks to nearby cells instead of every driver. Cell size must balance too many candidates in dense areas against searching many neighboring cells in sparse areas.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: A nearby-driver query scans 1,000,000 active drivers. Partition the map into cells and inspect only the rider's cell and its neighbors. Place Geo index, Candidates. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Rider → Geo index; Geo index → Candidates. That topology is the evidence for the answer: A geospatial index maps locations into cells, limiting exact distance checks to nearby cells instead of every driver. Cell size must balance too many candidates in dense areas against searching many neighboring cells in sparse areas.

exercises.prompt: 1 million drivers are online, each sending their location every 4 seconds. Roughly how many location writes per second?
exercises.why: One million drivers divided by a four-second update interval produces 250,000 location updates/sec before ride requests add load. The location path therefore requires sustained high write throughput and aggressive control of per-update work.

exercises.prompt: Should each of those 250,000 updates/sec be a row written to your main database?
choices: Yes — you need the location history
No: keep the replaceable current-location projection in a fast geo store, and archive trip samples through a separate durable stream
Only for drivers on a trip
exercises.why: The live projection keeps only the newest coordinate and can be rebuilt as drivers report again, so it belongs in a low-latency ephemeral geo store. Receipts, disputes, and safety workflows may need prior samples, so an asynchronous archival path durably stores trip history without putting those writes on the matching path.

exercises.prompt: Driver locations change constantly, are read constantly, and are worthless once stale. Add where they should live.
exercises.why: An in-memory location store supports frequent small overwrites and nearby-driver reads with low latency, and drivers rebuild its contents after failure. Durable trip records remain in an authoritative database because receipts, disputes, and payment workflows cannot be reconstructed from the next location update.

exercises.prompt: Split each location update into a fast matching projection and a durable trip-history path.
exercises.why: The geo store overwrites each driver's latest point for low-latency matching, while the durable stream carries ordered samples to trip-history storage asynchronously. If history storage slows, the stream buffers work and matching continues; putting archival writes inline would let a storage outage stall fresh-location updates.

exercises.prompt: Do all 250,000 updates/sec need to be processed at full fidelity?
choices: No: a driver parked at a red light is sending the same point repeatedly, so clients can throttle when stationary and send more often when moving fast
exercises.why: A stationary driver's frequent coordinates add little matching information, while a fast-moving driver's position becomes stale quickly. Adaptive reporting reduces redundant writes when movement is small and increases freshness when movement makes the old position inaccurate.

exercises.prompt: Why is this system harder than the news feed, despite the feed having more users?
choices: The feed was read-heavy and could precompute; this is write-heavy, real-time, and geographic — you can't precompute 'who's near me' because the answer changes every second
exercises.why: Nearby-driver results change continuously as drivers move and accept trips, so cached search results become stale quickly. The system must update and query a high-churn spatial index, which limits the benefit of conventional long-lived response caching.

exercises.title: A composite B-tree orders coordinates lexicographically
exercises.body: An index on `(latitude, longitude)` sorts first by latitude and uses longitude only among rows sharing the preceding latitude value. A latitude range can therefore span many unrelated longitudes, leaving the database to filter a large candidate set for a two-dimensional radius query.
exercises.note: Grid indexes such as Geohash encode regions as one-dimensional cell keys, enabling lookup of the containing cell and its neighbors before exact distance filtering.

exercises.prompt: A rider opens the app. You need drivers within 2km. Why can't a normal B-tree index on (latitude, longitude) do this well?
choices: A B-tree orders on one dimension at a time — it can find a latitude range, but every driver at that latitude anywhere on Earth qualifies, so you'd filter a huge set by longitude afterwards
The index would be too large
exercises.why: A B-tree on `(latitude, longitude)` is ordered primarily by latitude and only by longitude within equal latitude prefixes. A circular or box-shaped proximity query constrains both dimensions simultaneously, so this one-dimensional ordering scans many irrelevant entries.

exercises.prompt: So what's the core trick behind geospatial indexing?
choices: Reduce two dimensions to one: divide the world into cells and give each a single id, so 'nearby' becomes 'same or adjacent cell' — a one-dimensional lookup a normal index can serve
exercises.why: A geospatial cell encoding maps latitude and longitude into a one-dimensional cell key whose prefixes represent progressively smaller areas. The service can retrieve drivers in the rider's cell and neighboring cells, then apply an exact distance check.

exercises.prompt: Match each geospatial idea to what it does.

pairs.right: Encodes a grid cell as a string; a shared prefix means the same enclosing cell at that precision
Shorter prefix = bigger area = more candidates
Must be checked, or you miss drivers just over the border
Computed at the end, on the small candidate set

exercises.why: A shared Geohash prefix means two points fall within the same enclosing cell at that precision, not that every nearby pair shares a prefix. The query must include neighboring cells to catch boundary cases, then compute exact distance to remove false positives and order candidates.

exercises.prompt: Two drivers are 50 metres apart but on opposite sides of a cell boundary. What happens?
choices: A naive same-cell query misses one of them, because cell adjacency doesn't match real distance at the edges — so you must search the neighbouring cells too
exercises.why: Two nearby points can have different cell keys when a grid boundary lies between them. Querying adjacent cells prevents those boundary false negatives, and an exact distance calculation removes extra candidates introduced by the wider lookup.

exercises.prompt: Cell size is fixed. Downtown has 5,000 drivers in one cell; a rural cell has 2. What's the problem?
choices: Both ends break: the dense cell returns thousands of candidates to filter, and the sparse cell returns almost nobody — so a fixed grid can't serve both
exercises.why: A fixed cell creates large candidate sets and concentrated load in dense areas, while sparse areas may require searching many empty neighboring cells. Variable precision uses smaller cells for dense regions and larger cells for sparse regions to bound candidates and lookup expansion.

exercises.prompt: Should the geo index be sharded by driver id?
choices: No: every query asks 'who is near this point', so sharding by location keeps a query on one shard, while sharding by driver id would make every search hit every shard
exercises.why: Nearby-driver searches filter by spatial region, so location-based sharding routes a search to the relevant regional shards. Sharding by driver ID distributes writes but forces every proximity query to contact many shards; location sharding instead requires hotspot controls for dense regions.

exercises.title: Driver assignment needs an atomic, owned reservation
exercises.body: Each offer has a unique token. A matcher atomically changes `available` to a reservation containing driver, trip, token, and deadline. Acceptance succeeds only if all fields still match and the deadline has not passed.
exercises.note: Expiry and reassignment invalidate the old token, fencing a delayed acceptance from an offer that no longer owns the driver.

exercises.prompt: Two matchers read the same available driver and both assign that driver to different riders. Make driver assignment a single-winner operation.
exercises.beforeStatus: DRIVER D7 · assigned to Rider A and Rider B
exercises.afterStatus: DRIVER D7 · one claim wins · loser retries
exercises.result: Only one matcher can own the available-to-assigned transition
exercises.why: Use a conditional write or transaction that changes the driver from available to assigned only when the stored state is still available. The losing matcher receives zero updated rows or a conflict and searches again.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: Two matchers read the same available driver and both assign that driver to different riders. Make driver assignment a single-winner operation. Place Driver D7. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Matcher A → Driver D7; Matcher B → Driver D7. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Use a conditional write or transaction that changes the driver from available to assigned only when the stored state is still available. The losing matcher receives zero updated rows or a conflict and searches again.

exercises.prompt: Two riders request a ride simultaneously. Your matcher offers the same nearby driver to both. What have you built?
choices: A double-booking: the classic race — both matchers read 'driver available', both decide, and one rider gets a driver who's already gone
exercises.why: Both matchers read `available` before either writes the assignment, so each can offer the same driver to a different rider. This check-then-act race creates two commitments for one resource unless assignment is made conditional and atomic.

exercises.prompt: How do you make assignment safe?
choices: Atomically reserve the driver only if still available, recording the trip, unique offer token, and deadline
exercises.why: Compare-and-set changes `available` to a reservation containing its owner, unique offer token, and deadline. Exactly one concurrent matcher satisfies the condition; failed contenders choose another driver. Recording the token now also gives the later acceptance path a value it can fence after expiry or reassignment.

exercises.prompt: Does this need a distributed consensus service like ZooKeeper?
choices: Usually not: a conditional update in a store you already run gives you the mutual exclusion, and unit 20's advice was to use consensus only where two answers is a catastrophe you can't reconcile
exercises.why: The assignment changes one driver's record under one conditional predicate, which a database can enforce atomically on the authoritative key. A separate coordination service is unnecessary unless the invariant spans multiple stores or records that cannot be updated atomically together.

exercises.prompt: Your matcher assigns the nearest available driver, instantly, every time. What's wrong with that as a strategy?
choices: Nearest-now is greedy: waiting a moment to batch requests and drivers together often produces better overall matches than each decision made in isolation
exercises.why: Choosing the nearest driver independently for each request can consume a driver who is the only good option for another nearby rider. A short batching window allows joint optimization across several riders and drivers, trading added matching latency for lower total pickup time or higher match completion.

exercises.prompt: Offer A expires and the driver is reassigned with offer B. What prevents a delayed acceptance of A from stealing the driver back?
choices: The driver's phone clock rejects it
A unique offer token: atomically accept only when driver, trip, token, state, and unexpired deadline still match the reservation
exercises.why: The unique token identifies one reservation generation. Expiry or reassignment replaces that token, so the atomic acceptance predicate rejects a late message from offer A even if it arrives after offer B. A ride ID alone does not distinguish an obsolete offer from the current one, and a client clock cannot authoritatively decide server ownership.

exercises.prompt: The driver accepts, but the acceptance is lost in flight. What must be true of your system?
choices: It should retry the whole match
The client retries the same offer token; the server returns its stored result if that token already committed, and otherwise rechecks the fenced acceptance predicate
The rider is notified of failure
exercises.why: A lost acknowledgement leaves the app unable to tell whether acceptance committed. Retrying the same token is idempotent when the server records that token's result. If it already committed, return that result; if not, the server must atomically verify that the token still owns the live, unexpired reservation before accepting.

exercises.title: Consistency requirements are assigned per dataset and invariant
exercises.body: For each trip dataset, define the invariant that must hold, the tolerated staleness, and whether an incorrect result can be compensated. State that controls commitments needs coordination when concurrent updates could violate its invariant; telemetry can often tolerate bounded staleness.
exercises.note: Applying strong consistency to every update adds coordination to high-rate telemetry; applying eventual consistency to commitments permits conflicting outcomes.

exercises.prompt: The trip is underway. Which parts of this system now need strong consistency?
choices: All of it — it's a real-time system
Serialize local trip-state and ledger invariants; allow bounded map staleness only when it cannot authorize an irreversible action
exercises.why: Assignment state and local ledger entries represent exclusive or financial commitments, so concurrent local updates must be serialized to preserve their invariants. Map position and estimated arrival time can use bounded staleness when the display is advisory. This does not make an external card charge part of the same transaction; provider outcomes need a separate reconciled workflow.

exercises.prompt: At trip end, you must charge the rider and credit the driver — across your database and an external payments provider. What's the problem?
choices: Atomicity stops at your database: your `ROLLBACK` can't un-charge a card, so you need a saga with compensating actions plus idempotency keys
exercises.why: The local trip and ledger transaction can serialize internal invariants, but it cannot atomically commit with an external payment provider. The service records a payment intent, calls the provider with an idempotency key, and reconciles unknown outcomes; a later workflow failure uses a compensating action such as a refund.

exercises.prompt: A concert ends and 20,000 people request rides in one neighbourhood within two minutes. What breaks first?
choices: The geo partitions and matcher capacity serving that neighbourhood — spatial locality concentrates the surge in a small adjacent area
exercises.why: Location-based partitioning concentrates the neighbourhood's simultaneous searches and candidate updates in a small set of cells and their serving partitions; boundary-aware queries may touch several adjacent cells rather than exactly one shard. Finer subdivision, replicated read projections, adaptive update rates, and controlled admission can protect the localized hot area.

exercises.prompt: Which parts of this system can degrade gracefully during that surge? Select all.
choices: Showing fewer nearby drivers on the map
Updating the car's position every 8 seconds instead of every 2
Assigning the same driver to two riders
exercises.why: Lower map refresh frequency, delayed receipts, and coarser search precision reduce compute, writes, or fan-out while preserving core trip correctness. Allowing double booking violates the one-driver-to-one-active-trip invariant and therefore cannot be used as a degradation mode.

exercises.prompt: During the surge, your matcher is overloaded. Slide toward your response.
exercises.leftLabel: Queue every request; everyone eventually matches
exercises.rightLabel: Shed load: tell some riders 'no cars available, try again'
exercises.why: A long matching queue operates on locations and availability that may be stale by the time work begins, wasting capacity and returning poor assignments. Load shedding gives a timely failure when the system cannot meet its matching deadline and protects capacity for requests it can still complete.

exercises.prompt: Summarize the ride-sharing design.
choices: A geo database with real-time queries
Ephemeral live locations with durable history streaming; geo-cell lookup; fenced atomic offers; serialized local trip and ledger state; and reconciled idempotent provider payments
A microservices architecture with a message bus
A graph of drivers and riders
exercises.why: The design separates data by required guarantees: current positions use a high-throughput ephemeral spatial index, trip history is durable, assignments use conditional atomic updates, and payments use idempotent reconciled workflows. This prevents low-value location churn from imposing its scale on financial and assignment correctness paths.

exercises.title: Live location, matching authority, trip state, and payment have different correctness requirements
exercises.body: Location updates feed a spatial projection that may drop stale points. Matching claims one driver with an expiring, fenced offer. Accepted transitions advance an authoritative trip state machine, and payment uses a stable provider-facing operation identity because local and external state cannot commit atomically.
exercises.note: Do not assign one consistency label to the entire product. Nearby dots may be stale; one driver assigned to two riders and one trip charged twice violate hard invariants.

exercises.prompt: Matcher A's offer lease expires. Matcher B assigns the driver to another rider, but A's delayed acceptance arrives and overwrites B's newer assignment.
choices: Attach a monotonically newer offer token and reject transitions carrying an older token
choiceFeedback: Arrival order cannot distinguish current authority from stale work.
The trip store compares the token during the state transition and rejects stale ownership.
Longer leases delay reassignment but cannot eliminate delayed messages or crashed owners.
exercises.beforeStatus: OFFER A EXPIRED · OFFER B ACTIVE · late A steals driver
exercises.afterStatus: TOKEN A < TOKEN B · stale acceptance rejected
exercises.result: Expired matchers cannot mutate the current assignment
exercises.why: A lease limits how long an owner should act, but a delayed process may not know its lease expired. A fencing token travels to the authoritative state transition, allowing that resource to reject every operation from an older ownership generation.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: Matcher A's offer lease expires. Matcher B assigns the driver to another rider, but A's delayed acceptance arrives and overwrites B's newer assignment. Place Trip store. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Offer A · token 41 → Trip store; Offer B · token 42 → Trip store. That topology is the evidence for the answer: A lease limits how long an owner should act, but a delayed process may not know its lease expired. A fencing token travels to the authoritative state transition, allowing that resource to reject every operation from an older ownership generation.

exercises.prompt: Build the request-to-trip path while separating ephemeral location from durable trip history.
exercises.why: The spatial index narrows the search, the matcher evaluates current marketplace signals, and the reservation enforces one winner before authoritative trip creation. Analytics is downstream evidence, not assignment authority.

exercises.prompt: A review finds driver locations stored only in the trip database, nearest-driver selection with no reservation, wall-clock offer ordering, and a new payment key on each retry. Which failures follow? Select all.
choices: Location writes can overload durable trip storage
Two riders can receive the same driver
Clock skew and delay can revive stale offers
An ambiguous payment retry can charge twice
exercises.why: The design mixes high-volume ephemeral projection with durable state, omits single-winner assignment, trusts clocks for authority, and discards payment identity across retries. The complete trip path needs a different mechanism for each invariant.

exercises.prompt: Warehouse robots publish positions into spatial cells. A robot sits near a cell boundary. Why might a nearest-robot query inspect adjacent cells?
choices: The robot belongs to every cell
The nearest candidate can lie just across the boundary
exercises.why: Cell boundaries are indexing artifacts. A physically nearby candidate may be stored in a neighboring cell, so the query expands cells until its distance bound proves no closer candidate was omitted.
